notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Leviticus 26:1–23, drawing on the sources I could reach.

---

## Overall Structure

The chapter is widely recognised as a formal covenant document, patterned after ancient Near Eastern suzerainty treaties in which a king binds his vassals with blessings for loyalty and curses for rebellion (Enduring Word; Ellicott). It falls into four sections: foundational commands (vv.1–2), blessings for obedience (vv.3–13), curses for disobedience (vv.14–39), and a promise of restoration upon repentance (vv.40–46).

---

## v. 1 — Prohibition of Idols and Sacred Stones

**Traditional reading:** God begins the covenant not with blessings but with the first commandment's demand for exclusive worship. This is the "foundational law" — Yahweh alone must be worshipped (Enduring Word). Ellicott notes that in the Hebrew original, vv.1–2 belong to the previous section (Lev 25:47–55), where an Israelite sold to a heathen might be exposed to idolatry. Gill likewise notes the Jewish opinion (Jarchi, Aben Ezra) that the law is placed here to warn the Israelite sold to a stranger, though Gill himself sees it as placed here because idolatry is the "principal law" and breach of it "brought on all the calamities after mentioned."

The four terms — idols, carved image, sacred pillar, sculpted stone — are the "most comprehensive concentration of references to image making in the Bible, thus ruling out any type of idol worship" (Rooker, cited by Enduring Word). Ellicott explains the "standing image" (matzebah) as a plain, rude stone pillar, sometimes originally erected to God Himself (Gen 28:18) but later used for false deities. The "image of stone" (Hebrew maskith) was understood by second-Temple authorities as a figured or painted stone used for prostration in worship.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-26/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/26.htm
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/26.htm

**Denominational notes:** No significant tradition-specific differences emerged on this verse in the sources reached.

---

## v. 2 — Sabbath-Keeping and Reverence for the Sanctuary

**Traditional reading:** The two commands — keep My Sabbaths and reverence My sanctuary — are the practical expression of loyalty to Yahweh. They are paired with the idol-prohibition as the "two essential commandments of the Decalogue" (Ellicott). Ellicott notes these two commands are also joined (in reverse order) in Leviticus 19:3–4, and are repeated here precisely because the Israelite serving a heathen master was in danger of neglecting both. Gill observes that Aben Ezra restricts "Sabbaths" here to sabbatical years and "sanctuary" to the jubilee year, connecting the verse directly to Leviticus 25; but Gill himself takes it broadly as the weekly Sabbath.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/26.htm
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/26.htm

---

## v. 3 — The Condition: Walk in My Statutes

**Traditional reading:** This verse begins the blessings section. The condition is comprehensive — "walk in My statutes, keep My commandments, and do them" — covering moral, ceremonial, and judicial law (Gill).

**Reformed distinctives (Calvin):** Calvin offers an extended theological reflection here. He insists that the promise of reward on condition of obedience "would be ineffectual if He should be extreme in examining our works." The works of believers, though defective, are "pleasing to God through the intervention of pardon." Thus "to walk in the commandments of God" includes "the indulgence with which God regards His children and pardons their faults." Calvin also argues that the restriction of rewards to earthly, temporal blessings is part of the "elementary instruction of the Law" — just as Christ had not yet appeared, "so clear and familiar an acquaintance with eternal life…had not yet been attained by the Fathers as now shines forth in the Gospel." Temporal blessings were shadows pointing to spiritual realities.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-26.html
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/26.htm

---

## v. 4 — Rain in Season and Fruitful Land

**Traditional reading:** The first blessing is agricultural fertility. Ellicott notes that "your rains in due season" (the Hebrew plural) refers to the former rain (October–December, preparing the ground for seed) and the latter rain (March–April, just before harvest). This blessing also appears in Deut 11:14 and Ezek 34:26. Gill underscores that rain is a "principal blessing" which "only God, and not all the vanities of the Gentiles, could give." Calvin elaborates that God "might give us bread as He formerly rained down manna from heaven; but in order that the signs of His paternal solicitude may be constantly before us…the order of the seasons is so regulated that every day may renew the memory of God's bounty."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/26.htm
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/26.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-26.html

---

## v. 5 — Overwhelming Abundance and Security

**Traditional reading:** The harvests would be so plentiful that threshing (usually around March) would continue until the grape harvest (around July), and the vintage would continue until sowing time (October). This mirrors Amos 9:13: "the plowman shall overtake the reaper." Ellicott notes this is a picture of extraordinary corn and wine production. Gill adds that the promise includes not just plenty but also security: "plenty without safety would not be so great a blessing," since enemies could carry off their substance. The phrase "dwell in your land safely" adds the dimension of tranquillity.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/26.htm
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/26.htm

---

## v. 6 — Peace, Safety, and Removal of Wild Beasts

**Traditional reading:** Peace is promised in three dimensions: internal peace ("peace in the land"), personal security ("lie down, and none shall make you afraid"), and protection from wild animals and invading armies. Ellicott notes the promise to "rid evil beasts out of the land" is parallel to Ezek 34:25. Gill observes that "peace in the land" refers to freedom from insurrections, riots, and civil wars among themselves; the Jews (b. Taanith 22a) understood "neither shall the sword go through your land" to mean not even a foreign army passing through on its way to another country.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/26.htm
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/26.htm

---

## vv. 7–8 — Military Victory and Supernatural Ratios

**Traditional reading:** Victories would be so decisive that five Israelites would chase a hundred enemies, and a hundred would put ten thousand to flight. This is a "proverbial saying, corresponding to our phrase 'a mere handful shall be more than a match for a whole regiment'" (Ellicott). Enduring Word notes the "supernatural element": the ratio of 5:100 is one routing twenty, but 100:10,000 is one routing one hundred — an escalating, disproportionate blessing. Examples cited include Gideon's 300 defeating 135,000 Midianites, Jonathan and his armour-bearer defeating a Philistine garrison, and the four lepers whose sound terrified the Syrian army (2 Kings 7).

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/26.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-26/

---

## v. 9 — Fruitfulness, Multiplication, Covenant Confirmation

**Traditional reading:** "I will turn toward you" (better than "have respect unto you," per Ellicott) means God will show favour. The promise of fruitfulness and multiplication echoes the patriarchal covenant (Gen 12:2; 15:5; 17:2–6). Gill notes the covenant in view is "the covenant made with their ancestors concerning multiplication of their seed as the stars of heaven." The phrase "establish My covenant" confirms that obedience does not create the covenant but confirms it — the covenant originates in God's grace.

**Reformed (Calvin):** Calvin emphasises that God is said to "turn Himself" to those He undertakes to cherish; when He forsakes them, He is "turned away." He also notes that the covenant "is made void by our own fault" when we depart from God, citing Jeremiah 31:32.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/26.htm
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/26.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-26.html

---

## v. 10 — Old Store Cleared Out for New

**Traditional reading:** The blessing here is of such overflowing abundance that the previous year's grain must be removed from the barns to make room for the new crop. Gill notes the Hebrew suggests corn "of three years old" (Jarchi, Kimchi) — so much that it takes that long to consume. Calvin notes that this is "a great sign of abundance" because normally scarcity forces immediate use of new crops; here the old lasts until the new arrives.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/26.htm
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/26.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-26.html

---

## vv. 11–12 — God's Dwelling and Walking Among His People

**Traditional reading:** These are the climactic blessings. Material prosperity would be empty without God's presence. Ellicott notes that "I will set my dwelling-place among you" promises God will "permanently abide with them in the sanctuary." The promise "My soul shall not abhor you" means God does not regard it beneath His dignity to dwell among them. "I will walk among you" (v.12) is quoted by the Apostle Paul in 2 Corinthians 6:16 to describe the Church as God's temple (Enduring Word; Ellicott).

**Charismatic/Pentecostal (Guzik):** The emphasis falls on the relationship: "I will walk among you and be your God, and you shall be My people" is "the best promise" — if not for this, "all the material blessings described previously would be empty."

**Reformed (Calvin):** Calvin sees in "I will be your God" the hope of eternal immortality, because God is "the fountain of life, and not the God of the dead" (Matt 22:32). The earthly blessings were types; the true and solid felicity is spiritual.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-26/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/26.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-26.html

---

## v. 13 — Liberation from Egypt and Upright Walking

**Traditional reading:** The blessings section concludes with a reminder of past redemption — the exodus from Egypt — as the basis and motivation for obedience. Ellicott explains the imagery of "bands of your yoke": these are straight pieces of wood inserted in the yoke to fasten the heads of oxen together, representing the cruelty of Egyptian bondage. God broke these bands so Israel could "walk upright" — no longer stooped like slaves but erect with dignity. Gill sees this as a type of Christ's redemption: "as Christ has broken the yoke of spiritual enemies from off the shoulders and necks of his people."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/26.htm
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/26.htm

---

## vv. 14–15 — The Condition for Curses: Active Rejection of the Covenant

**Traditional reading:** The curses section (vv.14–39) is about twice as long as the blessings section. Enduring Word notes this "speaks to human nature, which is more motivated by the fear of threats than by the promises of blessing." The language escalates from passive indifference ("fail to obey," v.14) to active contempt: "reject My statutes, despise My ordinances" (v.15). Ellicott notes that what begins as "listlessness" develops into "contemptuous repudiation of God's ordinances." The verb "abhor" in "if your soul abhors My judgments" indicates a visceral loathing of God's law. Gill remarks that to despise them as unwise or unrighteous "is a dreadful reflection upon the Maker of them," and to abhor them is "shocking impiety."

**Reformed (Calvin):** Calvin argues that v.15 seems reserved for "ungodly and depraved apostates who deliberately revolt from the service and worship of God" — not those who fall through infirmity. However, he adds that "all sins betray contempt of the Law, and tend to break the covenant of God."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-26/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/26.htm
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/26.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-26.html

---

## v. 16 — First Cycle of Curses: Terror, Disease, and Vain Labour

**Traditional reading:** The first level of punishment (vv.16–17) includes "sudden terror" (possibly pestilence — Targum Jonathan), "wasting disease" (consumption), and "fever." Ellicott notes that the phrase "consume the eyes" is better rendered "extinguish the eyes" — the failing of sight — and "cause sorrow of heart" means "cause life to waste away." The agricultural curse reverses the blessing of v.4: instead of harvesting their own crops, enemies will eat them. This is the direct opposite of the promise in v.5.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/26.htm
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/26.htm

---

## v. 17 — God's Face Set Against Israel

**Traditional reading:** "I will set My face against you" means God will make them feel His active anger (Ellicott; cf. Lev 17:10). The result is military defeat, foreign domination ("those who hate you shall rule over you"), and psychological terror so profound that they "flee when no one pursues" — the exact reversal of the promise in vv.7–8. Gill notes this phrase is "the reverse of having respect to them" in v.9.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/26.htm
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/26.htm

---

## v. 18 — Second Cycle Introduced: "Sevenfold" Punishment

**Traditional reading:** This verse introduces the second and more severe cycle of curses (vv.18–20). The phrase "seven times more" does not mean a literal multiplication by seven but, using the number of completeness, means "indefinitely or unceasingly; many more times" (Ellicott). It signals that God's punishments are not arbitrary but proportioned to continued impenitence. Calvin emphasises the "gradation of punishments" — God first "lightly chastises" but increases severity when obstinacy is added. "Those who, being admonished, care not to repent, wage open war with God."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/26.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-26.html

---

## v. 19 — Pride Broken, Heavens like Iron, Earth like Bronze

**Traditional reading:** "The pride of your power" refers to the strength and wealth that produced Israel's arrogance. Ellicott notes that the authorities of the second Temple understood this phrase to denote the sanctuary itself (cf. Ezek 24:21, where the same Hebrew phrase is rendered "the excellency of your strength"). The Chaldee paraphrases: "I will break down the glory of the strength of your sanctuary." The imagery of "heaven as iron, earth as bronze" means the sky will yield no more rain than if it were metal, and the ground will be impenetrable. In Deut 28:23 the metals are reversed (heaven as brass, earth as iron), showing the same idea. This is the precise reversal of v.4's blessing.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/26.htm
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/26.htm

---

## v. 20 — Strength Spent in Vain

**Traditional reading:** All human labour — ploughing, digging, sowing — will be "perfectly useless" because no amount of effort compensates for withheld rain (Ellicott). This reverses the overflowing harvest of vv.5 and 10.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/26.htm

---

## v. 21 — Third Cycle: Walking in Hostility

**Traditional reading:** The third cycle (vv.21–22) is introduced with "if you walk in hostility toward Me." The Hebrew word keri is variously translated: the Chaldee takes it as "with hardness," Jerome as "in opposition to me," but Calvin argues for "at adventures" (fortuito) — meaning the sinner ascribes adversities to chance rather than to God's hand, producing "unconquerable obstinacy." Ellicott translates it as "continue in defiance of the Divine law and rebel against God's authority." The promise of multiplying plagues "according to your sins" indicates proportionality: the more they sin, the more they suffer.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/26.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-26.html

---

## v. 22 — Wild Beasts

**Traditional reading:** The third curse is destruction by wild animals — they will "rob you of your children, destroy your livestock, and reduce your numbers, until your roads lie desolate." This reverses v.6 where God promised to "rid the land of dangerous animals." Enduring Word notes one historical fulfilment in 2 Kings 17:25, where lions killed the settlers in Samaria because they did not fear the Lord. Ellicott notes that wild beasts abounded in Palestine (Exod 23:29) and are used throughout Scripture as instruments of divine punishment (Deut 32:24; Ezek 14:15).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-26/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/26.htm

---

## v. 23 — Fourth Cycle Introduced: Refusal to Accept Discipline

**Traditional reading:** This verse introduces the fourth cycle of curses (vv.23–26), which intensifies earlier punishments with pestilence, sword, and famine. Ellicott notes that "if you will not be reformed by Me" implies that God regards the preceding calamities as His discipline — correction meant to produce repentance. To refuse reformation is to reject God Himself. The phrase "walk in hostility toward Me" (keri) repeats from v.21, highlighting persistent defiance.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/26.htm

---

## Tradition-Specific Observations

**Reformed (Calvin):** Calvin's overarching framework is that the Law's temporal blessings and curses were "elementary instruction" for a people not yet fully acquainted with eternal life. Under the Gospel, God "does not openly take vengeance on sins as of old" because "the voice of the Gospel sounds much more clearly…summoning us to the heavenly tribunal of Christ." Believers under the New Covenant suffer affliction as "a manifest token of the righteous judgment of God" (2 Thess 1:5). Yet Calvin insists the promises still apply to believers because their imperfect obedience is accepted through divine indulgence. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-26.html)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik / Enduring Word):** Strong emphasis on the chapter's structure as an ancient Near Eastern treaty and on the New Covenant application: "Under the New Covenant, we are blessed not because of our obedience but because we are in Christ Jesus, who bore all the curse on the cross so we might receive the blessings of Abraham" (citing Gal 3:13–14). The material blessings of the chapter are not dismissed but seen as fulfilled spiritually and materially in Christ. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-26/)

**Baptist (Gill):** Gill's verse-by-verse exposition is more literal and detailed, interacting closely with Jewish sources (Jarchi, Aben Ezra, Kimchi, Targums). He often draws typological connections to Christ and the New Covenant, seeing the temporal promises as "emblems of spiritual things." For example, the rain in v.4 is an emblem of "the rain of divine grace, and the doctrines of the Gospel" (Deut 32:2), and the tabernacle in v.11 is "a type and emblem of the human nature of Christ." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/26.htm)

**Anglican (Ellicott):** Ellicott's commentary attends closely to the Hebrew text, translation issues, and historical context. He consistently notes the connection between Leviticus 26 and the preceding chapter (Lev 25), treating vv.1–2 as the conclusion of the section on the Israelite sold to a heathen. He also traces parallel passages in Ezekiel, Deuteronomy, and the prophets. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/26.htm)

**Dispensational (Gray):** James Gray's Concise Bible Commentary treats Leviticus 26 as "The Great Prophecy" — "an epitome of Israel's history from the death of Joshua…until the present time." He sees it as proof of the Bible's divine origin through its evidence of foreknowledge. Gray holds that the restoration promise (v.40) will be fully realised in the end times when Israel is restored to Palestine and to God through faith in her Messiah. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gray/leviticus/26.htm)
